title: US wind: what utilities and developers need to know
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Q3 2026 US wind monitor finds the five-year US onshore new-build forecast broadly stable because over half of the 2026-2028 pipeline is already operating or under construction, while policy, import restrictions and a new tornado-load code add cost and timing risk, and offshore diverges negatively.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's five-year US onshore wind new-build forecast has remained broadly stable quarter on quarter despite policy shifts.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Near-term US onshore wind volumes look less exposed to policy noise than headlines imply.

insights.claim: More than half of the 2026-2028 US wind project pipeline is already operational or under construction, limiting execution risk to the near-term outlook.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Advanced-stage projects give utilities and suppliers visibility; the risk sits in later-stage development.

insights.claim: Developers have accelerated US wind projects to capture remaining tax-credit opportunities, so commercial operation dates are shifting while the aggregate five-year outlook barely moves.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Expect timing volatility in COD rather than volume changes; watch quarterly installs for pull-forward effects.
insights.locator: Why is the US onshore wind outlook proving resilient?

insights.claim: The investable question in US wind is shifting from how much will be built to which projects are best positioned to reach operation and when.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Favor project-level maturity and location analysis over headline capacity forecasts.
insights.locator: Why is the US onshore wind outlook proving resilient?

insights.claim: Changes to permitting conditions have altered the risk profile for parts of the US wind pipeline.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Projects needing federal permits carry higher timing risk than those already permitted.
insights.locator: Why is the US onshore wind outlook proving resilient?

insights.claim: Import restrictions and pending guidance on the US wind supply chain leave developers with limited visibility on future sourcing strategies and costs.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Equipment cost and sourcing uncertainty is a margin risk for developers and an opportunity for domestic suppliers.
insights.locator: Why is the US onshore wind outlook proving resilient?

insights.claim: US firm wind turbine orders in Q2 2026 reached their highest quarterly level since late 2023 as developers secured equipment ahead of tax-credit qualification deadlines.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Order surge is a leading indicator for turbine OEM backlogs, though conversion to operating projects is unproven.
insights.locator: What does the latest turbine order activity indicate?

insights.claim: Policy timelines are increasingly driving US wind equipment orders, construction schedules and grid-connection strategies.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Track policy deadlines as the main driver of order and build cadence.
insights.locator: What does the latest turbine order activity indicate?

insights.claim: The West holds the largest share of Wood Mackenzie's US onshore wind new-build outlook through 2030, with Texas and the Midwest also significant.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Regional exposure matters for developers and utilities choosing procurement and siting.
insights.locator: Where are the biggest opportunities and risks emerging?

insights.claim: US offshore wind projects already under construction continue to advance, but an unstable policy environment and federal lease buybacks are shrinking the longer-term development pipeline.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: Offshore risk is a pipeline-depth problem beyond current builds; onshore and offshore should not be treated as one exposure.
insights.locator: Where are the biggest opportunities and risks emerging?

insights.claim: The forthcoming ASCE 7-28 building code guidelines are expected to extend tornado-load design requirements to wind turbines, potentially requiring more materials and raising project costs in tornado-prone regions.
insights.speaker: Diego Espinosa
insights.so_what: A new cost variable for wind siting in tornado-prone areas; watch turbine design and foundation cost implications.
insights.locator: Could new design standards change wind project economics?
